claims.claim: For plan year 2027, the individual-market open enrollment period on the federal platform runs November 1 through December 15.
Medicare Open Enrollment runs October 15 through December 7 each year.

For contract year 2027, CMS removed the prior 48-hour Scope of Appointment waiting period while retaining pre-appointment documentation requirements; applicable TPMO marketing, sales, and enrollment calls must be recorded.
Marketplace applicants should update income and household changes because those changes can affect coverage and premium tax credit amounts.
People who lose Medicaid or CHIP may be able to enroll in Marketplace coverage through a Special Enrollment Period, subject to current eligibility and timing rules.

Florida DCF may renew Medicaid automatically when available information supports eligibility; when additional information is needed, DCF sends renewal instructions about 45 days before the renewal date and says it will determine eligibility within 45 days after all required information is available.

Florida AHCA is seeking federal authority for a targeted Medicaid redetermination exemption involving specified permanently disabled recipients receiving institutional care, hospice, or qualifying home- and community-based services; the request is not a general exemption for all Medicaid recipients.

CMS says defined Medicaid adult populations must demonstrate community engagement beginning January 1, 2027, unless a state implements sooner. A qualifying month can include at least 80 hours of work, community service, a work program, qualifying education, or a combination, or earnings equal to 80 hours at the applicable federal minimum wage, currently $580 per month. Exclusions and hardship rules may apply.

Nebraska DHHS implemented Medicaid work requirements for new applicants in its Medicaid expansion category on May 1, 2026. Existing-member reviews begin with coverage periods ending on or after July 31, 2026, and Nebraska publishes exclusions and temporary-hardship rules.
Florida DCF determines family-related Medicaid income limits by coverage group and household size; a single income figure is not sufficient to determine eligibility.
Plan-specific Medicare provider, pharmacy, and drug review should use current Medicare Plan Compare and current plan documents for the exact plan year.

CMS states that the Medicare GLP-1 Bridge runs from July 1, 2026, through December 31, 2027. Eligible Medicare Part D beneficiaries have a $50 copay for certain weight-management GLP-1 drugs after program eligibility screening and prior authorization. The Bridge operates outside the Part D benefit payment flow; the Part D deductible does not apply and the copay does not count toward Part D true out-of-pocket costs. Eligibility, drug, formulation, and indication must be checked against current CMS criteria.

Federal Medigap Open Enrollment is a one-time six-month period beginning the first month a person has Medicare Part B and is age 65 or older; outside that period, medical underwriting may apply unless a guaranteed-issue right or another protection applies.

Medicare.gov states that some Medicare Advantage plans may have a $0 plan premium, while members generally must continue paying the Medicare Part B premium and plan-specific cost sharing still varies.
Medicare.gov lists the 2026 high-deductible amount for Medigap Plans F and G as $2,950.
The 2026 premium tax credit applicable percentage table ranges from 2.10 percent below 133 percent FPL to 9.96 percent from 300 through 400 percent FPL.

For tax year 2026, premium tax credit eligibility is generally limited to households with income from 100 percent through 400 percent of the federal poverty line, subject to the other tax, Marketplace enrollment, and minimum essential coverage requirements.

For 2025, the IRS Form 8962 instructions list excess advance premium tax credit repayment limits below 400 percent FPL by income band and filing status, including single-filer limits of $375, $975, and $1,625; at 400 percent FPL or above there is no 2025 limit.

For tax years after 2025, IRS guidance states that there is no repayment cap for excess advance premium tax credit; the full amount by which advance payments exceed the allowed premium tax credit is added to tax liability.

For plan year 2026 on the federal Marketplace platform, a consumer automatically re-enrolled with no premium responsibility after advance credits and without affirming or updating eligibility information is automatically re-enrolled with a $5 monthly premium; CMS states that the $5 amount is eliminated after the consumer confirms or updates the information and remains eligible for a $0 premium.

CMS recognizes that a Marketplace enrollee can have a $0 monthly premium after advance payments of the premium tax credit are applied; this outcome is household-, eligibility-, and plan-specific and is not a universal offer.

HealthCare.gov defines the premium as the monthly amount paid for coverage and states that deductibles, copayments, and coinsurance are additional costs; therefore, a $0 net premium does not mean health care has no other costs.

For employer plan years beginning in 2026, the affordability percentage is 9.96 percent; employee affordability uses self-only coverage while affordability for offered tax-family members uses the premium to cover the employee and all offered members of the tax family.

IRS Form 7206 instructions include a more-than-2% S corporation shareholder among taxpayers who may use the form to determine the self-employed health-insurance deduction, subject to the form's other eligibility and limitation rules.

Treasury Decision 9968 created a separate employer-coverage affordability test for related individuals based on the cost of covering the employee and offered tax-family members; the relevant provisions apply to taxable years beginning after December 31, 2022.
The current CMS Employer Coverage Tool collects minimum-value status and separate premium amounts for employee-only coverage and coverage of the employee plus offered members of the tax household.
A person who retires before age 65 and loses job-based coverage can apply for Marketplace coverage; eligibility and savings depend on the Marketplace application.
Losing job-based coverage can create a Marketplace Special Enrollment Period, subject to the current application, timing, and document requirements.
Marketplace applicants report estimated net self-employment income for the coverage year and may be asked for an accurate self-employment ledger or other supporting documents.
Current Marketplace instructions use the coverage-end date and eligibility notice to determine the enrollment and document deadlines after Medicaid or CHIP loss.

HealthCare.gov lists loss of qualifying coverage, specified household changes, and qualifying residence changes among events that may create a Special Enrollment Period. Timing, prior-coverage conditions, plan-category limits, and documentation vary by event, and the Marketplace application determines eligibility.

HealthCare.gov states that all 2026 Bronze and Catastrophic individual-market plans work with Health Savings Accounts. HSA contribution eligibility remains subject to the other federal eligibility rules, and HSA compatibility does not determine whether a plan is suitable for a household.

Florida OIR publishes plan-year 2026 individual-market premium tables and availability resources. Its percentage-change tables are market-level context and do not represent the change for a single policyholder or a household-specific quote.

CMS lists Florida individual- and small-group geographic rating areas by county, including Polk County as its own rating area. Current carrier, plan, and provider availability still must be checked for the exact application address, plan year, and plan.

The IRS states that the premium tax credit is generally the applicable second-lowest-cost Silver plan premium minus a percentage of household income, subject to eligibility rules and the enrollment-premium limit. The benchmark depends on the coverage family and residence and may differ from the enrolled plan.
A move outside a Medicare plan service area, or a move that creates new plan options, may create a Special Enrollment Period with timing based on when the plan is notified and when the move occurs.

People working past 65 should confirm how current employer coverage coordinates with Medicare; COBRA, retiree, Marketplace, and other non-current-employment coverage can follow different enrollment rules.

The current UnitedHealthOne Health ProtectorGuard brochure lists Florida, policy form HPG3-GRI-09, and the scheduled benefits and limits for Select 2000, Preferred 4000, and Premier 5000. The brochure is an outline; current ZIP-code availability, rate, underwriting result, and final terms require carrier and issued-certificate confirmation.

The current UnitedHealthOne Guard Plans brochure lists Florida, policy form HPG3-CSTM-GRI-09, and the scheduled benefits and limits for Guard 4000, Guard 5000, and Guard 6000. The brochure is an outline; current ZIP-code availability, rate, underwriting result, and final terms require carrier and issued-certificate confirmation.

For short-term, limited-duration insurance sold or issued on or after September 1, 2024, the 2024 federal final rule limits the initial contract term to no more than three months and the maximum coverage period, including renewals or extensions, to no more than four months.

On August 7, 2025, the Departments stated that they did not intend to prioritize enforcement of violations related to the 2024 STLDI definition while considering future rulemaking; the statement did not itself amend or repeal the final rule.

Florida Statute 627.6426 defines individual short-term health insurance as less than twelve months initially and no more than thirty-six months including renewals or extensions, and requires specified written purchaser disclosures. Federal requirements and enforcement posture must be evaluated separately.

For plan year 2026, the federal maximum annual limitation on cost sharing is $10,600 for self-only coverage and $21,200 for other-than-self-only coverage. A plan may use a lower limit, and the federal limit does not include premiums or every possible member expense.

For calendar year 2026, the HSA annual contribution limit is $4,400 for an eligible individual with self-only high-deductible health plan coverage and $8,750 for an eligible individual with family coverage. Eligible individuals age 55 or older may make the statutory additional $1,000 catch-up contribution.

For tax years beginning in 2026, the health FSA voluntary employee salary-reduction limit is $3,400. For cafeteria plans that permit carryover, the maximum carryover is $680; an employer plan is not required to permit carryover.
The Summary of Benefits and Coverage explains how a plan and member share costs, but it is a summary; the complete plan terms and applicable limitations and exceptions remain controlling.

Marketplace cost-sharing reductions lower deductibles, copayments, and coinsurance only when an eligible consumer enrolls in a Silver plan; the exact savings are determined after applying and shopping for Silver plans.

The Medicare card shows whether Part A, Part B, or both apply and when coverage begins. People with Original Medicare show the Medicare card for services, while people in Medicare Advantage use the plan card and keep the Medicare card secure.

For calendar year 2026, the general high-deductible health plan minimum deductible is $1,700 for self-only coverage and $3,400 for family coverage. Annual out-of-pocket expenses other than premiums may not exceed $8,500 for self-only coverage or $17,000 for family coverage.

Florida's approved plan-year 2026 individual-market table reports a 34.1% membership-weighted average premium increase based on 2025 enrollment. It is a statewide market measure, not the change for every household or policy.
If a parent's health plan covers dependents, a young adult usually can be added and remain covered until age 26; Marketplace and job-based enrollment timing and plan rules differ.

Catastrophic Marketplace plans may be available to people under age 30 and to certain older applicants meeting current exemption rules; they cover essential health benefits and at least three primary-care visits before the deductible, and premium tax credits cannot be applied to them.
